access.coverageNote: No live walk of the Hers consultation was possible at any of the three stages: the site stays behind a security checkpoint, which was not defeated. No answer was changed and replayed, so nothing in this file is 'observed'. What the file holds is (1) Hers's stated safety and eligibility policy, from patient leaflets in the shared Hims & Hers help centre (opened directly and re-read word for word at stage 3) and from Hers pages read only through a search index; (2) descriptions of the quiz by reviewers and one partner article (2023 to Nov 2026), now labelled 'inferred' because they are not Hers's own statements; (3) one code hint: names of old Hers hair experiments in the page state served by the sister site. Stage 3 check: Innerbody (Dec 2023) says oral minoxidil 'starts at $29/month' in 1.25 mg and 2.5 mg; finvsfin (Aug 2026) and NCOA (Oct 2026) give 1.25 mg rising to 2.5 mg. products.recommendedWhen: Not observed. From Hers's documents: for an adult woman with female pattern hair loss who is not pregnant, not breastfeeding and not planning a pregnancy, and has no pheochromocytoma (help centre leaflet, re-read word for word at stage 3); a history of heart problems must be told to the provider (same leaflet). Hers product pages, read only through a search index, add that it may not suit people with kidney or liver disease or blood pressure problems. A search summary of Hers's treatment terms page (/treatment/hair-loss/oral-minoxidil) says people under 18, people with pheochromocytoma and people already using minoxidil products are not eligible through the platform and are pointed to in-person care. A sentence saying oral minoxidil is not offered for telogen effluvium or alopecia areata was found by the search engine only on a copy of the page on another Hers host (internal.forhers.com), so it is not confirmed for the public page. Whether the quiz steers a patient to plain tablets or to a vitamin blend is unknown. The provider sets the dose: 1.25 mg to start, 2.5 mg possible (reviews).

engineSummary: Untested: the site was blocked at all three stages, so this is how the engine should work according to Hers's own public statements and reviewers, not how it was seen to work. Hers treats one diagnosis, female pattern hair loss, with one main drug, minoxidil, sold in several formats. (1) A short visual quiz collects goals, symptoms, hair density and routine; nothing public shows these changing the product. (2) Health questions, either inside the quiz (2023 report) or in an intake form after it (2025 and 2026 reports), feed three documented gates. Menopause: finasteride (the Postmeno Serum) is only for women past menopause. Pregnancy, planning a pregnancy or breastfeeding: oral minoxidil in any form and finasteride are ruled out. Health: pheochromocytoma rules out oral minoxidil and a heart history must go to the provider (confirmed word for word in the help centre); kidney, liver and blood pressure problems, age under 18 and already using minoxidil are further exclusions read only through a search index. (3) A preference question reported in 2023 (vitamins with your treatment?) probably picks between plain oral minoxidil at $29 a month and the vitamin blends at $35 to $39. (4) One or two prescription products are shown, reportedly after an account is made, and can be swapped; a licensed provider then approves, changes or declines and sets the dose, by message in most states and by video in some. Over-the-counter minoxidil, supplements and hair care sit outside the quiz. Spironolactone may no longer be part of the hair range.
strengths: Many formats of one proven drug: plain oral minoxidil, three minoxidil plus vitamin formats (pill, chew, gummy) and a topical serum, so almost any preference can be met without changing the active ingredient.
A clear, defensible finasteride rule (after menopause only), with a dedicated postmenopausal product.
Low entry price: $29 a month for oral minoxidil and over-the-counter minoxidil from $12.67 a month on a long plan.
The patient can swap the suggested treatment before the provider sees it (reported), and pays nothing until a treatment is selected.
Written patient information for every prescription product is public in the help centre, and compounded products are clearly labelled as not FDA-approved.
Narrow scope: Hers is reported to say it does not offer oral minoxidil for telogen effluvium or alopecia areata (sentence found only on a non-public copy of the page; not confirmed).
weaknesses: The quiz result sits behind an account (reported), so a visitor cannot see a recommendation or a final price without giving contact details.

The consultation is reported as thin on cause-finding: no reviewer mentions questions on thyroid disease, iron or anaemia, PCOS or signs of high androgens, recent illness or weight loss, scalp symptoms, family history, contraception or period regularity. No blood tests and no blood pressure reading are described, although the main drug is a blood pressure medicine.
Most prescription products are compounded and not FDA-approved, and the strengths of the oral blends are not published on the pages found.
Eligibility rules are scattered: exclusion lists sit on separate treatment terms pages (/treatment/hair-loss/...), apart from the product pages (pages not opened; from search-index reads).

No source shows dutasteride, oral finasteride for women, tretinoin add-ons or iron or vitamin D testing in the range. Spironolactone, the usual anti-androgen tablet for women before menopause, appears in no 2023 to 2026 description of the hair range, and one 2026 reviewer says Hers does not offer it.
Prices are hard to pin down: sources give $35 and $39 for the blends, $39 and $50 a month for the postmenopausal spray, and plan-length prices are only shown inside the flow.
Reviewers are said to report complaints about subscription charges, refunds and reaching a clinician (stage 1 reading; not re-checked at stage 3).
opportunities: Show the recommendation, strength and full price before asking for an email or an account.
Ask the cause-finding questions Hers is not reported to ask (thyroid, iron, PCOS signs, recent illness, scalp symptoms, medicines that cause shedding) and explain how each answer changed the plan.
Offer a route for the women Hers's stated policy leaves out: sudden shedding, patchy loss, pregnancy and breastfeeding (advice, safe topicals, blood tests, referral).
Ask for a home blood pressure and pulse reading before oral minoxidil, and say so up front. If offering spironolactone (Hers appears not to today), include a potassium check plan.
Publish who cannot have each treatment on the product page itself, and state exact strengths for combination products.
Give perimenopausal women a clear answer: Hers's finasteride rule is 'after menopause only', with nothing specific in between.
Sell fewer, simpler options with fixed, visible plan prices; Hers's many near-identical minoxidil formats are hard to compare.

Every rule is Hers's stated eligibility or safety policy (docs) or reasoning from it (inferred). The documents say who should not have a product; they do not say whether the quiz blocks the patient, hides the product, shows a warning or leaves it to the provider.
Question wording is not verbatim and most answer options are unknown. Options shown as 'implied' or 'reviewer's category' are not the site's wording.

Prices come from a search index and from reviews of different dates and disagree in places; plan-length prices for prescription products were not found.
The default product for any profile is unknown; the 'offered' lists in recommendations are the products the patient is eligible for on paper, not a seen result.

verification.verdict: Trust this report as a map of Hers's published policy and product range, not as a description of its quiz. The site was blocked at all three stages, so no answer was ever changed and replayed and nothing is observed. The safety rules that rest on the help-centre leaflets (finasteride not before menopause; no oral minoxidil in pregnancy, when planning one or when breastfeeding; pheochromocytoma; heart history to the provider; provider decides; video visit in some states) were re-read word for word and are solid as policy. The product list is broadly right for the five core prescription products and the over-the-counter items, with prices good to within a few dollars and several strengths unknown. The quiz outline is second-hand, partly three years old, and three of its questions have no traceable source. Spironolactone and the spray may no longer be sold. After the stage 3 corrections the labels are honest: 'docs' means Hers, its help centre or a partner article says so (sometimes read only through a search index, which is flagged each time); 'inferred' covers reviewer reports and reasoning. A reader should not use this file to say what any single answer does in the Hers quiz.
